6. The historical background of the challenge is that in 1982 the Government made a policy decision to invest Executive Magistrate with sweeping judicial powers to try criminal cases, not just petty offences, but even offences not punishable with death or with transportation or with imprisonment for a term exceeding ten years. The legislative expression of that decision was given by inserting a new section in the Code of Criminal Procedure, section 29C, contained in the Code of Criminal Procedure (Second Amendment) Ordinance, 1982 (Ordinance No. XXIV of 1982), promulgated on 21.8.82 Section 29C was as follows:—" 

 29C Offences not punishable with death. Notwithstanding anything contained in section 29, the Government may invest the District Magistrate, Additional District Magistrate or any Magistrate of the first class with powers to try as a Magistrate all offences not punishable with death or with transportation or with imprisonment for a term exceeding ten years." Something more was done by the same Ordinance. A proviso was added to sub-section (3) of section 9 Cr.P.C., as follows:— 

 "29C. Offences not punishable with death.- Not withstanding anything contained in sector 29 the Government may—(a) invest the District Magistrate or any Additional District Magistrate with power to try as a Magistrate all offences not punishable with death (b) invest any Magistrate of the first class with power to try as a Magistrate all offences not punishable with death or with transportation or with imprisonment for a term exceeding ten years." The provisos to sub-section (3) of section 9 and sub-section (4) of section 31, however, remained unchanged and so they remain till to-day. By Notification No.ED/FA-28/83-120 dated 6.3.83 the Government invested all Additional District Magistrates with powers to try as Magistrates all offences not punishable with death. Consequently, all Assistant Sessions Judges of the country are now deemed to have been appointed as Additional Sessions Judges. 

 21. The substance of the submission of the learned Attorney-General is that it is a cardinal rule of interpretation that a proviso to a particular provision of a statute only embraces the field which is covered by the main provision. The main sub-section (3) of section 9 provides that the Government may also appoint Additional Sessions Judges and Assistant Sessions Judges to exercise jurisdiction in one or more such Courts i.e. Courts of Session only. Assistant Sessions Judges, deemed to have been appointed Additional Sessions Judges by virtue of the proviso, will only exercise jurisdiction in the Court of Session and that was the only purpose of his appointment. It was the burden of the learned Attorney-General's submission that the word 'jurisdiction' referred to in sub-section (3) of section 9 is limited to trial of cases. It does not cover appeal, revision, review and reference. Referring to the 'deeming' provision, the learned Attorney-General submits that the only thing that is 'deemed' in the proviso is the appointment of the Assistant Sessions Judge as Additional Sessions Judge. Read with the main sub-section, he can only exercise trial jurisdiction and pass higher sentences under section 31(4). The learned Attorney-General has also traced the legislative history o the amendments and has argued that the intention of the legislature in effecting these amendments was to obtain a speedy trial of criminal cases. The Assistant Sessions Judge has no power of hearing appeal, revision, review and reference and if he passes a sentence of imprisonment for a term of five years or less the appeal will lie to the Court of Sessions, as before. 

 "9(1) The Government shall establish a Court of Sessions for every sessions division, and appoint a judge of such Court ; and the Court of Sessions for Metropolitan Area shall be called the Metropolitan Court of Session." 

 35. Section 9(1) needs to be analyses a Lillie closely. By establishing a Court of Session for every Sessions Division, the Government constitutes a class of Criminal Court, mentioned in section 6(1); for the purpose of trial of criminal cases as a Court" of original jurisdiction. But by appointing a judge of such Court, the Government docs not constitute a Court, it creates an office. The Court of Session is a Criminal Court, but the Sessions Judge, appointed to man the Court, is an office. Throughout the Code, the legislature maintains a sharp and obvious distinction between the Court of Session and the Sessions Judge. One is a Court, the other is an of five. They are not interchangeable. They do not mean the same thing. This will be evident from various other provisions of the Code to which we shall refer in due course. 

 Section 9(2) in as follows:- "9(2) The Government may, by general or special order in the official Gazette, direct at what place or places the Court of Session shall hold its sitting; but, until such order is made, the Courts of Session shall hold their sittings as heretofore." 

 Then comes section 9(3) which is as follows:- 9(3) The Government may also appoint Additional Sessions Judges and Assistant Sessions Judges to exercise jurisdiction in one or more such Courts : Provided that wherein a district, the District Magistrate, Additional District Magistrate or any Magistrate of the first class is specially empowered under section 29C to try any offence, all Assistant Sessions Judges of the Sessions division, within which the district is situate shall be deemed to have been appointed as Additional Sessions Judges of that division. 

 In order to understand the implication of the proviso to sub-section (3) of section 9 we have to understand what in precisely meant by the main sub-section. When the Government appoints an Additional Sessions Judge and an Assistant Sessions Judge under sub-section (3) of section 9, it does not constitute an Additional or Assistant Sessions Court. There can be only one Judge of such Sessions Court and that is the Sessions Judge. If an Additional Sessions Judge is appointed, he can try only such cases, which, under section 193(2) of the Code, the Government by general or special order may direct him to try or the Sessions Judge of the Division, by general or special order, may make over to him for trial. If an Assistant Sessions Judge is appointed, then under section 17(3) of the Code, he shall be subordinate to the Sessions Judge in whose Court he exercises jurisdiction. The Sessions Judge will dis- tribute business among the Assistant Sessions Judges. In order words, the Additional and Assistant Sessions Judges do not have any independent jurisdiction of their own. 

 37. Sub-section (3) of section 9, it should be next remembered, is not a definition clause of Additional Sessions Judge and Assistant Sessions Judge. This sub-section does not define these offices at all. It is only an enabling sub-section authorizing the Government to appoint certain judicial officers to man the Court of Session other than the Sessions Judge. 

 38. The next point to remember is that this sub-section does not spell out the precise jurisdiction of the Additional and Assistant Sessions Judges. The Government may appoint them "to exercise jurisdiction in one or more such Courts." But the exact jurisdiction that they will exercise will have to be found out from some other provisions of the Code. 

 41. We have seen earlier that under section 9 (1) the Government establishes a Court of Sessions for every Sessions division and appoints a Judge of such Court, but section 9(1) does not state or describe the powers and functions of such Court. Section 28, occurring in the same Part 11, explicitly confers the power of trial to the Court of Sessions. Without this conferment, the Court of Session was only a constituted Court without definite power. 

 Provided that an Additional Sessions Judge shall hear only such appeals as the Government may, by general or special order, direct or as the Sessions Judge of the division may make over to him." 

 97. An argument has also been advanced by Messers Mujibur Rahman and his associates that if the application of the proviso in question does not extend to the provisions of Chapters XXXI and XXXII of the Code, with regard to appeals, revisions and references, that will lead to an anomalous situation, in view of the fact that under the provisions of the Code, as it now stands, the District Magistrate and the Additional District Magistrates have been vested with the appellate authority under sections 406, 406A and 407 and with provisional authority under sections 435, 436 and 438 of the Code in certain matters, although the Assistant Sessions Judges, who are sufficiently qualified to deal with such appeals and revision cases will be debarred from exercising such appellate and revision authority under the Code. The learned Advocates sought to argue that the Code of Criminal Procedure (Second Amendment) Ordinance 1982 (Ordinance No. XXIV of 1982), which has introduced the aforesaid proviso to section 9(3) has also amended the provision of section 407 of the Code deleting the express provision of section 407(2) of the. Code of hearing appeals by the Assistant Sessions Judges, as the legislature was well aware that no such provision needs to he kept in the Code, since in view of the proviso to section 9(3) those Assistant Sessions Judges under the deeming clause, henceforth are vested with the authority of hearing appeals, being the Additional Sessions Judges. 98. The changes in the provisions of sections 407 and 409 of the Code, sometimes allowing the Assistant Sessions Judges to hear appeals, to be preferred before the Court of Sessions or to the Sessions Judge have got a chequered history. Identical provision, as it now stands for section 407, had been in the old Code regarding hearing of appeals by the District Magistrate or any other Magistrate of First Class subordinate to him and empowered by the local government to hear such appeal on the order of conviction passed by a Magistrate Second Class or Third class of any person sentenced under section 349 by the then Sub-divisional Magistrate of Second Class. With a view to paving the way of separating the judicial and executive functions of the Magistrates in the then province of East Pakistan, now comprising Bangladesh, the then Provincial Assembly of East Pakistan on the 11th of November 1957 passed the Code of Criminal Procedure (East Pakistan Amendment) Act, 1957 and thereby omitted the provision of section 407 and substituted the original provision of section 409 of the Code as hereunder:--"409. Subject to the provisions of this section, an appeal to the Court of Sessions Judge shall be heard by the Sessions Judge or by an Additional Sessions Judge or an Assistant Sessions Judge : Provided that an Additional Sessions Judge shall hear only such appeal as the Provincial Government may, by general or special order, direct or as the Sessions Judge of the Division may make over to him Provided further that no such appeal shall be heard by an Assistant Sessions Judge unless the appeal is of a person convicted on a trial held by any Magistrate of Second class or Third class." 99. Thus, by virtue of such amendment the Assistant Sessions Judges were expressly invested with the appellate authority to hear certain appeals from the order of conviction that would be passed on a trial by the Magistrate, second class or third class. But before coming into force of such Act, under the President's Rule in the then East Pakistan, pro-claimed on the 25th June, 1958, under Article 193 of the Constitution of the then Islamic Republic of Pakistan, in exercise of the powers conferred by Article 102 of the said Constitution, the then governor on the 26th July, 1958 promulgated the Code of Criminal Procedure (East Pakistan Third Amendment) Ordinance, 1958 (East Pakistan Ordinance No LXIV of 1958); which was given effect- retrospectively with effect from the 23rd day of July, 1958, amending the provision of section 407 of the Code, substituting the words "District Magistrate" in sub-section (1) thereof by the words "Sessions Judge" and substituting the former sub-section (2) thereof making provision for the Assistant Sessions Judges to hear certain criminal appeals under the Code. The relevant provisions of that Ordinance may for information be quoted as hereunder : 2. Section 407 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898, in its application to East Pakistan shall have, during the period specified in section 3, effect as if, in sub-section (1) thereof for the words "the District Magistrate", the words "Sessions Judge" were substituted and for sub-section (2) thereof the following were substituted, namely :—"(2) The Sessions Judge may direct that any appeal under sub-section (I) or any class of such appeals shall be heard by any Additional Sessions Judge or any Assistant Sessions Judge of the Sessions Division." 3. The period referred to in section 2 in respect of any area is the period beginning with the date of commencement of the Code of Criminal Procedure (East Pakistan Amendment) Ordinance, 1958, and ending with the date on which the provision of the Code of Criminal Procedure (East Pakistan Amendment) Act, 1957 is brought into force in such area. 4. Any appeal of a person convicted on a trial held by any Magistrate of the second or third class, which immediately before the commencement of the Code of Criminal Procedure (East Pakistan Amendment) Ordinance, 1958 was pending before any District Magistrate or any Magistrate subordinate to him and which stood transferred to the Sessions Judge of the Sessions Division as from the date of commencement of that Ordinance, shall be heard by him or he may transfer such appeal to such Additional Sessions Judge or such Assistant Sessions Judge, as he thinks fit, for hearing." 100. Before making such changes 'in 'section 407 there were other changes in the Code vide East Pakistan Ordinance No. XII of 1958 and the East Pakistan Ordinance No. XXXII of 1958. Later on only section 6 of the aforesaid Ordinance No. LXIV of 1958, which had repealed the Code of Criminal Procedure (East Pakistan Second Amendment) Ordinance, 1958 (East Pakistan Ordinance No XXXIII of 1958) was repealed by the East Pakistan Ordinance No. XIII of 1966. Thus, before bringing a drastic amendment, in the Code by the Code of Criminal Procedure (Second Amendment) Ordinance, 1982 (Ordinance No. XXIV of 1982), which came into force on the 21st day of August, 1982, section 407 of the Code since 23rd July, 1958 had been in force as hereunder :—"407.—(1) Any person convicted on a trial held by any Magistrate of the Second or third class, or any person sentenced under section 349 or in respect of whom an order has been made or a sentence has been passed under section 380 by a Sub-divisional Magistrate of the second class, may appeal to Sessions Judge. (2) The Sessions Judge may direct that any appeal under sub-section (1) or any class of such appeals shall be heard by any Additional Sessions Judge or any Assistant Sessions Judge of the Sessions Division." 101. It also appears that for West Bengal, in India, the State Government of West Bengal Act 60 of 1950 amended the original provision of section 407 of the Code empowering the Sessions Judges to transfer to any Assistant Sessions Judge, subordinate to them, any appeal presented to the Court of Sessions and thereupon such Assistant Sessions Judges would hear such appeal. At present however, in India there is no provision like 407 of our Code, instead, in the original section 409 of the Code, which has been renumbered as section 381, provisions have been made to hear and dispose of certain criminal appeals by the Assistant Sessions Judge, to be preferred against conviction on a trial held by a Magistrate of the second class, under certain conditions mentioned therein. Thus, changes in the provision of section 407 of the Code might have been brought in the then Province of East Pakistan by the aforesaid Code of Criminal Procedure (East Pakistan Third Amendment) Ordinance, 1958 (East Pakistan Ordinance No. XLIV of 1958) empowering the Assistant Sessions Judges to hear and dispose of certain criminal appeals to be preferred in the Court of Session, in the light of what had earlier been brought for the State of West Bengal in India by West Bengal Act 60 of 1950. 102. It is interesting to note that in the then Province of East Pakistan, now comprising Bangladesh, although certain bold steps were taken in 1957 amending section 409 of the Code, pointed above, making provisions thereunder to hear and dispose of certain criminal appeals by the Assistant Sessions Judges by the then Code of Criminal Procedure (East Pakistan Amendment) Act 1957 (East Pakistan Act No. XXXVII of 1957) after deleting the provision of section 407 of the Code, but for obvious reasons the same was not allowed to take effect Instead the East Pakistan Ordinance No. LXIV of 1958, mentioned earlier, made the provision in section 407 empowering the Assistant Sessions Judges to hear certain criminal appeals by making amendment thereof in sub-section (2). 

 103. Thus, evidently since 23rd of July, 1958 till 21st of August, 1982, when the Code of Criminal Procedure (Second Amendment) Ordinance, 1982 was promulgated by the then Chief Martial Law Administrator, the Assistant Sessions Judges were empowered to hear and dispose of certain criminal appeals, mentioned in that section 407 of the Code. 

 105. Moreover, under the proviso to section 409 of the Code the Government may by general or special order, direct the Additional Sessions Judges to hear certain appeals which are required to be preferred to the Court of Sessions or the Sessions Judge. Had it been the intention of the legislature to allow disposal of the appeals by the Assistant Sessions Judges, certain provisions would have been made for the Government to confer upon those Assistant Sessions Judges in accordance with the provision of section 39 of the Code by its executive orders for the disposal of such appeals. But no such provision has been made.
